title: Asthma: Confirm Variable Airflow Disease, Then Step Treatment
bottomLine: Asthma requires a compatible variable respiratory syndrome plus objective evidence of variable airflow limitation when feasible. Use ICS-containing controller therapy, confirm adherence/technique/triggers before stepping up, and treat severe exacerbations according to acuity rather than waiting for outpatient confirmation.
recognize: Episodic wheeze, cough, dyspnea or chest tightness that varies with time/triggers supports asthma.
Normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma; repeat testing or another validated demonstration of variability may be needed.
differentiate: COPD has persistent obstruction in the appropriate exposure context; inducible laryngeal obstruction, HF, anxiety, GERD and eosinophilic bronchitis can mimic symptoms.
assessment: Assess symptom frequency/night waking, exacerbations/systemic steroids, triggers, smoking/vaping, occupation, atopy, inhaler technique/adherence, pregnancy and comorbidity.
workup: Use spirometry with bronchodilator response and other objective variability testing when needed; do not rely on symptoms alone for a stable long-term diagnosis when testing is feasible.
management: Use current CTS ICS-containing stepwise therapy matched to control/exacerbation risk; address inhaler technique, adherence and triggers before unnecessary escalation, and step down carefully after sustained control.
medicationSafety: LABA should not be used as asthma monotherapy; repeated oral corticosteroid exposure carries substantial cumulative toxicity and should trigger controller/severe-asthma review.
counselling: Provide a written asthma action plan and teach controller versus reliever roles plus inhaler technique.
followUp: Reassess control, exacerbations, technique and objective lung function; refer severe/uncontrolled or diagnostically uncertain disease.
examTrap: Increasing asthma medication repeatedly without verifying technique/adherence—or prescribing LABA alone because symptoms improved previously with bronchodilation.
oneLinePearl: Confirm variability, use ICS-containing therapy, and fix delivery/adherence before assuming treatment failure.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2021 asthma guideline update

title: COPD: Confirm Persistent Obstruction and Treat Symptoms/Exacerbation Risk
bottomLine: COPD requires compatible symptoms/exposure plus persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction. Treatment is driven by symptoms and exacerbation history, with long-acting bronchodilation, smoking cessation, vaccination and pulmonary rehabilitation; ICS is added selectively, not automatically.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, chronic cough/sputum and tobacco/occupational/biomass exposure are typical.
Exacerbation frequency and prior hospitalization predict future risk and should influence treatment intensity.
differentiate: Asthma shows greater variability and changes the ICS safety strategy; HF, ILD, anemia and deconditioning can mimic COPD symptoms.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency should be considered/tested according to current CTS guidance rather than only in extremely young nonsmokers.
assessment: Assess exposures, symptoms/function, exacerbations, oxygenation, weight/frailty, cardiovascular disease, inhaler technique/adherence and eosinophilic/asthma features.
workup: Confirm persistent obstruction with post-bronchodilator spirometry; use imaging/full PFTs when another diagnosis, complication or disproportionate symptoms are present.
management: Use CTS-guided LAMA/LABA strategies according to symptom/exacerbation burden; add ICS when appropriate to exacerbation/asthma/eosinophilic context, and use pulmonary rehab/smoking cessation/vaccination.
medicationSafety: ICS can increase pneumonia risk in selected COPD patients; repeated short-acting-only treatment is inadequate chronic management for symptomatic disease.
counselling: Teach inhaler/device technique, exacerbation action plan and smoking cessation without stigma.
followUp: Track symptoms/exacerbations, spirometry when useful, oxygen need and rehab/advance-care needs.
examTrap: Diagnosing COPD from smoking history alone without stable spirometric confirmation—or adding ICS to every COPD regimen automatically.
oneLinePearl: COPD is confirmed obstruction plus a symptom/exacerbation phenotype, not simply age plus smoking.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2023 COPD pharmacotherapy guideline

title: Interstitial Lung Disease: Recognize Restriction, Crackles, and Exposure/Autoimmune Clues
bottomLine: Progressive dry cough/exertional dyspnea, fine inspiratory crackles, restrictive physiology or fibrotic imaging should trigger ILD evaluation and early respirology referral. Define exposures, medications and connective-tissue disease before labeling idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
recognize: Fine bibasilar crackles, clubbing, exertional desaturation, restriction/reduced DLCO and HRCT interstitial patterns are clues.
Bird/mould exposure, occupational dusts, autoimmune symptoms, radiation and drugs can identify a treatable cause.
differentiate: HF, emphysema, obesity/neuromuscular restriction and chronic infection can mimic parts of the presentation.
An acute ILD exacerbation or infection can rapidly worsen a previously stable fibrotic disease.
assessment: Assess tempo, oxygenation/exertional desaturation, exposures, connective-tissue symptoms, medication/radiation history, smoking, reflux/aspiration and functional decline.
workup: Use full PFTs/DLCO and HRCT; order autoimmune/exposure testing by phenotype and coordinate multidisciplinary/specialist assessment for classification.
management: Remove harmful exposures/drugs, treat the specific inflammatory/fibrotic disease through specialty care, use rehabilitation/oxygen when indicated, and address transplant/palliative planning in advanced disease.
medicationSafety: Before immunosuppression, perform infection screening/vaccination review according to current CTS guidance; antifibrotic/immunosuppressive therapies require drug-specific monitoring.
counselling: Discuss exposure avoidance, vaccination, rehabilitation and why specialist classification matters before disease-specific drug therapy.
followUp: Trend symptoms, PFT/DLCO, oxygenation and imaging only at clinically meaningful intervals; coordinate specialty care.
examTrap: Calling every restrictive spirometry pattern ILD—or calling fibrotic ILD idiopathic before asking about autoimmune disease, drugs and exposures.
oneLinePearl: ILD is a pattern that demands a cause search and early specialist classification.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society ILD current standards/2026 immunosuppression infection-screening statement

title: Pulmonary Embolism: Probability, Imaging, Hemodynamic Risk, Anticoagulation
bottomLine: PE evaluation begins with clinical probability. Use D-dimer to exclude selected low/intermediate-risk patients, definitive imaging when indicated, and hemodynamic/RV risk to determine disposition and reperfusion urgency; anticoagulation choice/duration depends on provoking factors, bleeding risk and patient context.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, syncope or hemoptysis may occur; presentation can be subtle.
Shock/hypotension, RV strain and myocardial injury markers identify higher-risk physiology.
differentiate: Pneumonia, ACS, pneumothorax, HF and anxiety can mimic PE.
A positive D-dimer does not diagnose PE and a low D-dimer is not the appropriate rule-out strategy when pretest probability is high.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, oxygenation, DVT signs, prior VTE, cancer, surgery/immobility, hormones/pregnancy, bleeding risk and renal function.
workup: Use validated probability plus D-dimer/imaging strategy; pregnancy requires pregnancy-adapted imaging/diagnostic pathways. Evaluate RV strain/biomarkers for confirmed PE severity when relevant.
management: Start anticoagulation for confirmed PE and selected high-probability cases when appropriate/safe; high-risk PE with shock needs urgent expert reperfusion assessment, while stable low-risk patients may qualify for outpatient care under a validated pathway.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant selection requires renal function, pregnancy, cancer, drug interactions and bleeding context; thrombolysis is not routine for every PE.
counselling: Teach anticoagulant adherence/bleeding precautions and recurrence signs; discuss provoking factors and duration plan.
followUp: Reassess anticoagulation duration, post-PE symptoms and possible CTEPH when dyspnea persists.
examTrap: Using a positive D-dimer as the diagnosis—or giving thrombolysis to every CT-confirmed PE regardless of hemodynamic risk.
oneLinePearl: PE care is probability first, then confirmation, then hemodynamic risk.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada pulmonary embolism clinical guides

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Diagnose the Sleep Disorder, Then Make PAP Usable
bottomLine: OSA requires a compatible clinical syndrome plus objective sleep testing; snoring alone is not the diagnosis. PAP treatment succeeds only when mask/interface, pressure, nasal symptoms, adherence barriers and residual sleepiness are actively reviewed rather than simply prescribing a machine.
recognize: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas/gasping, daytime sleepiness, resistant hypertension, AF and obesity raise suspicion, but OSA occurs across body sizes.
Children may present with behavioural/learning problems rather than classic adult sleepiness.
differentiate: Insomnia, insufficient sleep, narcolepsy, medications, depression and central sleep apnea can cause fatigue/sleepiness.
Obesity hypoventilation includes awake hypercapnia and requires a different ventilation assessment.
assessment: Assess sleep schedule, witnessed breathing events, driving/work risk, nasal obstruction, medications/alcohol, cardiometabolic disease, pregnancy and craniofacial/tonsillar factors.
workup: Use validated home sleep apnea testing or polysomnography according to pretest probability/comorbidity/local pathway; current CTS/CSS pediatric OSA guidance applies to children.
management: Use CPAP/APAP when indicated, address weight/position/nasal/upper-airway contributors, and refer dental/surgical options selectively. Review device data and patient experience to improve adherence.
medicationSafety: Sedatives/alcohol/opioids can worsen sleep-disordered breathing; untreated severe sleepiness changes driving/occupational safety.
counselling: Frame PAP problems as solvable equipment/comfort issues rather than noncompliance; teach cleaning and mask-fit basics.
followUp: Review symptoms, adherence/device data, residual events/leak and cardiometabolic risk; reassess diagnosis when PAP fails despite good use.
examTrap: Diagnosing OSA from snoring alone—or declaring CPAP treatment failure without reviewing mask leak, pressure, nasal symptoms and actual device use.
oneLinePearl: OSA needs objective diagnosis, and PAP needs active troubleshooting to become effective treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society/Canadian Sleep Society sleep-disorder guidance

title: Pleural Effusion: Is It Expected, Unexplained, Infected, or Malignant?
bottomLine: A pleural effusion is a finding, not a diagnosis. Bilateral effusions in clear HF may improve with decongestion, but unilateral, atypical, febrile, recurrent or unexplained fluid generally requires imaging and diagnostic thoracentesis to distinguish transudative from exudative/infected/malignant disease.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic pain, reduced breath sounds and dullness can occur; small effusions may be incidental.
Pneumonia/empyema, malignancy, PE and inflammatory disease commonly cause exudates; HF/cirrhosis can produce transudates.
differentiate: Not every HF effusion requires immediate tap, but unilateral fever/pleuritic pain should not be dismissed as HF.
Complicated parapneumonic fluid/empyema needs drainage strategy, not antibiotics alone.
assessment: Assess heart/liver/renal disease, infection, malignancy, PE, autoimmune disease, medications, weight loss and oxygenation.
workup: Use ultrasound/chest imaging and diagnostic thoracentesis when indicated; classify using accepted pleural-fluid criteria and order cultures/pH/cytology/other tests based on the differential.
management: Treat cause, drain symptomatic/complicated collections as appropriate and urgently manage empyema, hemothorax or respiratory compromise.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulant/procedure risk using local protocols rather than one universal cutoff.
counselling: Explain why fluid analysis can be necessary even if drainage temporarily improves symptoms.
followUp: Track cytology/culture/imaging and resolution to a named cause; recurrent unexplained fluid needs specialist evaluation.
examTrap: Assuming unilateral febrile pleural fluid is 'from heart failure' without diagnostic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Pleural fluid becomes clinically useful when you ask why it is there.

title: Hemoptysis: Stabilize the Airway, Then Find the Source
bottomLine: Hemoptysis severity is defined by airway/hemodynamic threat more than a memorized volume. Distinguish true lower-airway bleeding from GI/nasopharyngeal sources, stabilize significant bleeding, then evaluate infection, malignancy, bronchiectasis, PE, TB and anticoagulation.
recognize: Blood-streaked sputum can be minor; rapid ongoing bleeding can obstruct the airway before it causes exsanguination.
Smoking/age/weight loss, TB exposure, anticoagulation and bronchiectasis change the differential.
differentiate: Hematemesis is GI; posterior epistaxis can mimic hemoptysis.
Life-threatening hemoptysis is functional—gas exchange/airway/hemodynamics—not one volume threshold.
assessment: Assess ABCs, oxygenation, bleeding rate, airway protection, anticoagulants, cancer/TB/VTE risk, infection and prior lung disease.
workup: Use chest imaging/CT and bronchoscopy/interventional evaluation according to stability and suspected source; obtain CBC/coagulation/type-cross and microbiology as clinically indicated.
management: Life-threatening bleeding needs emergency airway positioning/interventional management and appropriate anticoagulant reversal; treat the cause and do not leave recurrent unexplained hemoptysis without imaging follow-up.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants/antiplatelets can worsen bleeding but stable minor bleeding still requires balancing the indication before reflex cessation.
counselling: Any recurrent or increasing hemoptysis needs reassessment even if a prior episode was called bronchitis.
followUp: Close imaging/bronchoscopy/microbiology findings until cause and follow-up ownership are documented.
examTrap: Focusing on estimated millilitres while the patient's airway is filling with blood.
oneLinePearl: In major hemoptysis, protect the airway first; the exact volume can wait.

title: Chronic Cough: Medication, Airway, Upper Airway, Reflux, or Red Flag?
bottomLine: Chronic cough needs a structured cause search rather than repeated antibiotics. Review ACE inhibitors/smoking, chest imaging/red flags and common causes such as asthma/eosinophilic airway disease, upper-airway disease and reflux, while recognizing TB, ILD, bronchiectasis and malignancy when the pattern does not fit.
recognize: ACE inhibitors, smoking/vaping, asthma, upper-airway cough syndrome and reflux commonly contribute.
Hemoptysis, weight loss, fever, clubbing, abnormal imaging or significant dyspnea change the urgency.
differentiate: Postinfectious cough can persist after acute infection; chronic productive cough with recurrent infections suggests bronchiectasis/COPD rather than simple postviral cough.
Reflux treatment is most convincing when reflux features are present; indiscriminate prolonged PPI trials can delay another diagnosis.
assessment: Define duration/productivity/triggers, smoking/vaping, medications, nasal/allergy/asthma/reflux symptoms, occupational exposure, TB risk and red flags.
workup: Use chest radiograph and spirometry as appropriate, then cause-directed bronchoprovocation, CT, ENT or GI evaluation rather than shotgun testing.
management: Treat the most plausible cause with a time-limited response plan; stop ACE inhibitor when appropriate, manage airway/rhinitis/reflux disease and escalate abnormal imaging/red flags.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated antibiotics/opioid antitussives without a defined indication; chronic cough treatment should not obscure a serious cause.
counselling: Set expectations that cough evaluation may require sequential therapeutic trials with explicit stop/reassess points.
followUp: If cough persists despite adequate cause-directed therapy, revisit the differential and refer rather than recycling the same treatment.
examTrap: Giving a third antibiotic for chronic cough without reviewing ACE inhibitor use, asthma, upper-airway disease, reflux and chest imaging.
oneLinePearl: Chronic cough is an algorithm, not an antibiotic indication.

title: Tuberculosis: Test the Right Risk, Exclude Disease, Treat Infection or Disease Correctly
bottomLine: TB infection testing is targeted to people with meaningful exposure/progression risk and a plan to act on the result; TST/IGRA do not diagnose active TB disease in adults. Symptoms/imaging suggesting active disease require respiratory specimens/molecular/culture evaluation, airborne precautions and public-health coordination before preventive therapy is considered.
recognize: Risk assessment includes close contact, residence/travel in high-incidence settings, immune suppression, congregate exposures and structural/social determinants.
Active pulmonary TB can present with cough, fever/night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis or abnormal imaging and may be less symptomatic with immune suppression.
differentiate: TB infection (positive TST/IGRA without active disease) and TB disease require different testing/treatment and infection-control responses.
Canadian Standards discourage testing low-risk populations and using TST/IGRA to support active-disease diagnosis in adults/adolescents >12.
assessment: Assess symptoms, exposure/epidemiology, immune status, pregnancy, prior TB/testing/treatment, medications and barriers to care.
workup: For suspected active pulmonary TB use chest imaging and appropriate respiratory NAAT/smear/culture with susceptibility testing; for infection use TST or IGRA only when indicated and first exclude active disease before preventive treatment.
management: Active TB requires multidrug expert/public-health-managed treatment and adherence/support; TB preventive treatment uses a current Canadian regimen selected for interactions, comorbidity and patient preference.
medicationSafety: Rifamycins have major drug interactions; isoniazid/pyrazinamide/rifampin can cause hepatotoxicity and ethambutol requires vision monitoring in active-disease therapy. Regimens/monitoring must follow current TB standards/public-health program.
redFlags: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB in healthcare/congregate setting
counselling: Use culturally safe non-stigmatizing communication and explain why infection testing is targeted rather than universal; address housing, transport and medication-access barriers.
followUp: Coordinate public-health contact investigation, adherence/toxicity monitoring and post-treatment respiratory follow-up; Canadian Standards recommend PFT assessment after pulmonary TB treatment.
examTrap: Calling a positive IGRA active TB—or ordering IGRA as the diagnostic test for an adult with symptoms and cavitary lung disease.
oneLinePearl: TST/IGRA detect TB infection; active TB disease needs microbiology/imaging and public-health action.
sourceBasis: Canadian Tuberculosis Standards 8th edition — Diagnosis of TB Infection, Diagnosis of TB Disease, Treatment of TB Disease and Preventive Treatment
